This week on Dezeen , we reported on the Lion Green Road housing scheme in Croydon winning the Stirling Prize .

Designed by local studio Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, the project was named the UK's best new building at a ceremony in London.

Commissioned by Croydon Council, the development contains 157 homes spread across five blocks that are connected by a series of shared green spaces.

Following the win, we discussed the project and its place within the wider Stirling Prize winners on our podcast , Dezeen Weekly.

This week also saw car brand Tesla unveil its flying Roadster at an event in Texas , where the vehicle flipped off a ramp and briefly flew.

The demonstration used compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claimed will enable it to make the world's quickest production car.

In design news, technology brand Apple unveiled HomeView , a device that consolidates the functions of its app products and home-management software into one device.

The seven-inch screen, which can also stand on a base with an integrated speaker, was designed to function as a centralised location for home controls.

- Pieces feature diverse tectonic explorations incorporating solid walnut, curved aluminium, dark brown cork, plywood, and leather fabricated in Lisbon, Portugal.

CONTENT:
US architecture studio Baird Architects has released its inaugural furniture collection, with seating, tables, and shelving, designed by in-house architects and collaborators and made in Portugal.

The twelve-piece BA Objeto collection was led by Baird Architects founder Matthew Baird, who designed several pieces and also commissioned studio employees and collaborators.

Each piece is credited to its designer, and the designers will receive a portion of the profits, according to Baird.

The works include a solid walnut "surf" table by Baird, a swooping aluminium coffee table by Ines Gulbenkian and a dark brown cork bench by Gina Jiang.

The pieces are primarily produced in Lisbon , Portugal, where Baird Architects has established a new studio to support its furniture making.

Baird said a "considered approach to materiality, a crisp aesthetic, and a desire to push the boundaries of furniture design" draws the collection together.

The move points to an expansion of the studio's work beyond one-off furniture creation and illustrates a different business model for architecture studios.

CONTENT:
Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India , with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site.

The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events.

Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings.

"The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen.

"The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added.

Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape.

TITLE: Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant
SOURCE: Dezeen Interiors
CATEGORY: INTERIOR_NEWS
ARCHITECT/MANUFACTURER: Formant Studio
TYPOLOGY: Hospitality
LOCATION/CLIMATE: Escandón I, Mexico City, Mexico
MATERIALS & FINISHES: Mexican rosewood, Kvadrat upholstery textiles, Black-stained oak, Polished grey terrazzo, Natural stone pillars, Steel
SUMMARY:
- Formant Studio transformed a historic hacienda-style residence into Nota Tavern, an Italian-American restaurant in Mexico City marrying Chicago tavern aesthetics with modernist influences.
- The interior specification features custom Mexican rosewood paneling and banquettes, black Kvadrat textiles, black-stained oak furniture, polished grey terrazzo flooring, and unpainted restored stone pillars.
- The spatial plan utilizes double-height volumes and an inserted mezzanine dining room above the kitchen, creating defined acoustic and visual zones within the preserved structural envelope.
CONTENT:
Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence.

Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant.

It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion.

Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode.

"The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity," Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen.

"The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language."

Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city.

Lots of well-known actors, musicians, and athletes have properties in Manhattan. And developers have long responded to the perceived needs of these celebrities by crafting buildings offering porte cocheres so they can arrive and depart in secret, private elevators to whisk them to their apartments without encountering anyone, and discreet staff who help minimize their contact with the city itself.

Julianne Moore, wearing Bottega Veneta and an ear cuff by Messika, looks out from her window-wrapped kitchen. Fashion styling by Kate Young.

Julianne Moore is not of that ilk. The actor and her husband, film director Bart Freundlich, have always been engaged downtown New Yorkers. They raised their two children in the West Village, first in a loft and then in a town house with a beautiful garden (created with designer Brian Sawyer), which was featured twice in AD . Both homes were renovated and refined by her brother-in-law, AD100 architectural designer Oliver Freundlich. And each of them was infused with Moore’s passion for design.

In this lecture, Ayaz Basrai explores drawing as a way of thinking, not just a way of recording, tracing how the act itself can reveal how the mind constructs and misremembers what it sees. He sees drawing as a bridge into unfamiliar ways of perceiving, whether human, ecological, or computational, and concludes with a sense of cautious optimism speculating where emerging technologies might take the practice next.

MORII DERO by MORII DARSHAN is one of six projects that emerged from the mentorship of the Godrej Design Lab Fellowship in 2025. The fellows exhibited their projects and processes at the Concious Collectiv e in December 2025.

A portable textile tent, Morii Dero extends the craft-led practice into an interpretive process blending field-led research, designer-artisan collaboration. Using a stitch library and digitising processes, appliqué, Sujni embroidery, and block-printing, artisans translate natural forms into layered textiles. Freestanding, reassemblable, and foregrounding lineage, and the emotional resonance of hand-made environments, Morii Dero reimagines an archetype as an introspective textile space.

Morii Darshan is a Gandhinagar-based studio grounded in the knowledge, rhythm, and intelligence of hand embroidery. Working with over 180 artisans across twelve villages in India, the studio’s practice grows out of field-led engagement, observing, learning, and documenting stitch vocabularies from clusters in Bihar, Kutch, and Bengal. Design Pataki > A New Kind of Retreat: Swastik’s Approach to Regenerative Wellbeing

When it comes to well-being, we often look for quick fixes: a hack, a treatment, an hour at the spa, essentially temporary indulgences that offer immediate relief before we return to our lives. A massage or spa day may leave us restored, but the effect can be fleeting. If the intention is lasting change, perhaps what we need is not another escape, but a chance to regenerate.

At Swastik Wellbeing Sanctuary , regeneration is at the heart of the experience. Rather than offering a temporary reset, the sanctuary takes a holistic approach to detox, designed to restore internal balance, build mental resilience and reconnect us with our vitality. By slowing down and stepping away from the routines that leave us depleted, the aim is to re-engineer how we live, so we don’t always need to escape to feel our best. Founded by Dr. Nitin Nyati and directed by Anushree Nyati, Swastik envisions wellbeing as a “lifelong journey of transformation rather than a temporary escape.”
